questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of chronic kidney failure?

options.text: Diabetes
Excessive exercise
Dehydration
Kidney stones

questions.explanation: Diabetes is one of the most common causes of chronic kidney failure. High blood glucose levels damage the tiny blood vessels in the glomeruli, gradually reducing the kidneys' ability to filter blood effectively.

questions.stem: In haemodialysis, which principle is used to remove waste products from the blood?

options.text: Ultrafiltration under high pressure
Active transport across the membrane
Osmosis into the dialysis fluid
Diffusion down a concentration gradient

questions.explanation: In haemodialysis, waste products like urea diffuse from the blood (high concentration) across a semi-permeable membrane into the dialysis fluid (zero urea concentration), moving down their concentration gradient.

questions.stem: Why does the dialysis fluid contain glucose at normal blood concentration?

options.text: To add extra glucose to the patient's blood
To prevent glucose from diffusing out of the blood
To provide energy to the dialysis machine
To help dissolve the urea in the fluid

questions.explanation: The dialysis fluid contains glucose at normal blood levels so there is no concentration gradient for glucose. This means there is no net movement of glucose out of the blood, ensuring the patient does not lose this essential nutrient.

questions.stem: What is one major advantage of a kidney transplant over dialysis?

options.text: It offers a better quality of life with fewer restrictions
It does not require any medication afterwards
It never fails once the transplant is complete
It is available immediately without waiting

questions.explanation: A successful kidney transplant offers a much better quality of life than dialysis. Patients do not need time-consuming dialysis sessions and have fewer dietary restrictions, allowing them to live more normally.

questions.stem: Why must patients take immunosuppressant drugs after a kidney transplant?

options.text: To increase blood flow to the new kidney
To prevent blood clots forming in the new kidney
To help the new kidney produce more urine
To stop the immune system attacking the transplanted kidney

questions.explanation: The immune system recognises the transplanted kidney as foreign tissue and may attack it (rejection). Immunosuppressant drugs reduce the immune response to prevent this, but must be taken for life and increase the risk of infections.

questions.stem: How often does a patient typically need haemodialysis?

options.text: Every day for 8 hours
Once a week for 30 minutes
Once a month for 1 hour
Three times a week for 3-5 hours

questions.explanation: Haemodialysis is typically needed three times a week, with each session lasting 3-5 hours. This is time-consuming and can significantly impact a patient's lifestyle, work, and travel.

questions.stem: What is one consequence of kidney failure if left untreated?

options.text: The lungs stop producing carbon dioxide
Red blood cells increase in number
Urea accumulates in the blood, causing toxic effects
The liver stops making bile

questions.explanation: When the kidneys fail, they can no longer filter urea from the blood. Urea and other waste products accumulate, becoming toxic and causing symptoms such as confusion, nausea, and potentially coma or death if untreated.
